title: Secret Service Cracks Down on Card-Skimming Scams That Cost Americans Over $1 Billion Annually
excerpt: Federal agents removed more than 400 illegal skimming devices from ATMs, gas pumps, and point-of-sale terminals nationwide in 2025, preventing an estimated $428 million in fraud losses.
body:
• The U.S. Secret Service inspected nearly 60,000 card readers and removed 411 illegal skimming devices during 22 operations across major cities in 2025
  • Card skimming costs U.S. financial institutions and consumers more than $1 billion annually, with EBT fraud disproportionately targeting low-income communities
  • FICO data shows over 243,000 debit cards were compromised by skimming in 2025, a 5% increase from 2024, with 90% of incidents at non-bank ATMs
  • The Secret Service warns that criminals are adapting, reinstalling devices within hours of their removal, and selling stolen data on the dark web

The U.S. Secret Service has escalated its war against card-skimming fraud, conducting a sweeping nationwide campaign that removed hundreds of illegal devices from payment terminals and prevented an estimated $428.1 million in consumer losses during 2025.

Working alongside federal, state, and local law enforcement partners, the agency inspected nearly 60,000 point-of-sale terminals, gas pumps, and ATMs across 22 operations in cities from Los Angeles to New York. The effort uncovered 411 illegal skimming devices — small electronic gadgets criminals install to secretly capture card data from unsuspecting consumers.

A Growing Threat to Vulnerable Communities

Card skimming remains a persistent and evolving threat, costing U.S. financial institutions and consumers more than $1 billion each year. The crime is particularly devastating for recipients of government assistance programs. Criminals target Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) cards, timing their fraudulent withdrawals around monthly benefit deposits to drain accounts before recipients can use the funds.

"When you think of an individual recipient getting $300 to $1,200 per month in food benefits, and you divide that into the $428.1 million in potential losses, you are talking about hundreds of thousands of people that would not have been getting their benefits."

— Michael Peck, Assistant Special Agent in Charge, Secret Service Criminal Investigative Division

Over 670,000 households receiving SNAP assistance had their benefits stolen between 2023 and 2025, with the federal government replacing more than $320 million in stolen funds. Propel, a company providing a mobile app for benefit management, estimates criminals stole $349 million in the first half of 2025 alone.

How the Scam Works

Criminals install small, often undetectable devices inside ATMs, gas pumps, and merchant terminals. These skimmers capture card information when a magnetic stripe is swiped. Tiny pinhole cameras may also be placed above keypads to record PIN entries. The stolen data is then encoded onto blank cards with magnetic strips — sometimes hotel key cards — or sold to other criminals on the dark web.

The scheme is alarmingly efficient. Secret Service Financial Analyst Vincent Porter said agents frequently find devices that business owners never knew existed. In one Boston operation, a bakery owner broke down in tears upon learning a skimmer had been victimizing his customers.

The problem extends beyond small businesses. A 2025 FICO report showed that over 243,000 debit cards were compromised by skimming that year, a 5% increase from 2024. Approximately 90% of incidents occurred at non-bank ATMs, including terminals in convenience stores and gas stations. More than 3,500 financial institutions were affected.

Criminals Adapt Quickly

Perhaps most troubling is the speed at which criminals operate. Porter noted that within days or even hours of agents educating store owners about skimming threats, scammers returned to install new devices. The short lifespan of each skimming operation — with 64% lasting one week or less — makes detection and prevention extremely difficult.

Romanian organized crime networks have been particularly active. Between 2023 and 2024, the FBI and Department of Justice conducted multiple operations targeting Romanian nationals linked to skimming rings, including an operation that targeted 84 sites, resulting in 48 arrests and the seizure of over 8,000 stolen card numbers.

How to Protect Yourself

The Secret Service recommends several precautions: inspect card readers for loose, crooked, or damaged components before use; opt for tap-to-pay or chip technology whenever possible; shield PIN entry with your hand; and avoid using ATMs in poorly lit or isolated locations. At gas stations, running a debit card as credit avoids PIN entry entirely.

"These operations are only the start. We are working closely with our local, state, federal and international law enforcement partners to investigate and dismantle the criminal organizations that perpetrate these crimes."

— Kyo Dolan, Assistant Director, Secret Service Office of Field Operations

The agency has pledged to continue its outreach operations into 2026, with field offices in Houston, Dallas, Pittsburgh, and other cities already conducting additional sweeps this year. The Houston operation alone netted 14 illegal devices and prevented an estimated $14.5 million in losses.
